transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-06-12 15:00 UTC | Duration: 52 minutes | Recording id: ff-20260612-tdw-001
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Carlos Rivera (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Tidewater - Head of ML), James Holloway (Tidewater - Platform Eng), Elena Park (Tidewater - Finance)

Auto-summary: customer evaluating Redwood for an internal document-summarization pipeline; main constraints are cost per token, latency under 300ms p50 for short summarizations, and budget cap for Q3 pilot. They are SOC 2 in flight and need VPC/kms.

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I see we have Priya, James and Elena; I think we captured the goals in the invite but quick round robin 30 seconds each?
[00:12] Priya Nair: Yeah hi, Priya here, Head of ML at Tidewater. We're building a summarization and extraction layer across docs, main ask is keep unit economics low because we'll be doing millions of small requests, and we care about latency for user-facing flows.
[00:26] James Holloway: James, platform, I'll own infra questions — VPC, network, logging, identity.
[00:31] Elena Park: Elena, finance, I'll be looking at the budget and procurement cadence.
[00:35] Maya Chen: Great. Carlos and I are from Redwood — Carlos will help on sizing and benchmarks. Quick note, this call is discovery so we'll try to map constraints to deploy options: Hosted, Dedicated reserved pools, or Private/VPC on prem.
[00:49] Carlos Rivera: Hi all. Priya, can you give a sense of prompt lengths, avg token counts and qps? Even ballpark helps us pick batch sizes and cache strategies.
[00:58] Priya Nair: Sure. Summaries are typically 250–400 tokens input, responses 40–120 tokens. QPS expected 50 bursts up to 200, avg 20. We expect mostly short, many concurrent users.
[01:12] Carlos Rivera: Okay that profile is helpful; short outputs so latency matters. On Hosted we can optimize with continuous batching, and prefix/KV caching helps if you have repetitive contexts. For per-token economics, batching reduces amortized overhead but increases tail latency; so we tune batch windows.
[01:29] Priya Nair: Can you give a rough cost comparison? We ran numbers versus OpenAI and Vertex, but they didn't show dedicated options.
[01:36] Maya Chen: Yeah rough rule of thumb: hosted per-token price plus data transfer, but with batching and cache you can often cut per-token cost by 20–55% depending on hit rate. Dedicated gets you reserved throughput at lower per-token, especially with quantized model variants. Private/VPC has higher TCO upfront but gives control for compliance and sometimes cheaper at scale because you manage hardware.
[01:55] Elena Park: We're constrained for Q3 pilot to a fixed spend of $80k — that's the cap for any external vendors. Is that sane to hit for a meaningful pilot?
[02:04] Carlos Rivera: Totally plausible. For example if you run a 2k-request benchmark with batching and 30% cache hit, we can project unit econ. We'll send a worked example.
[02:15] James Holloway: How deterministic are the numbers? I mean latency fluctuations, and the fallback behavior if capacity is saturated — do you have auto-fallback to smaller models?
[02:24] Carlos Rivera: We have routing policies: latency-first or cost-first. If capacity is constrained we can route to a lower-cost compatible model; there are also canary rollouts. For latency concerns, Dedicated with pinned model versions reduces variability.
[02:39] Priya Nair: Can you explain KV cache vs prefix cache? We saw notes in docs but some of our prompts are unique per user so hit rate might be low.
[02:48] Carlos Rivera: Sure — prefix cache stores token sequences for identical prefixes; KV cache is for transformer head cache reuse across tokens in multi-turn. For summarization, if inputs are highly variable, prefix cache helps less; KV caching can still speed up autoregressive sections if you reuse contexts. If customer has templated prompts, cache hit is higher.
[03:07] Maya Chen: Also worth noting quantization — 4-bit quantized variants reduce GPU cost and can lower per-token substantially, but may affect quality for very sensitive extract tasks. We typically run a quick eval to see quality delta.
[03:20] Priya Nair: OK. Another constraint: we are SOC 2 Type II in flight and require SSO + SAML, audit logs, and KMS for key management. Does Redwood cover that in Hosted?
[03:30] Maya Chen: Yes Hosted supports SSO/SAML for console access, and we provide audit logs and encryption at rest; KMS integration for Dedicated and Private is supported — we'll share the SOC 2 report and runbook. For strict regulatory needs Private/VPC is common.
[03:44] Elena Park: Procurement question — if we go Dedicated, what's the contract shape? Upfront commit? Monthly?
[03:50] Maya Chen: Dedicated is reserved capacity with monthly or annual commits. We can structure a quarter-long pilot as a short commitment or trial — we have flexible pilot options that don't require full annual commit. We'll include options in the pricing sheet.
[04:03] James Holloway: Network egress and data residency: we need logs to stay in our VPC and 3rd party can't exfiltrate. With Hosted, is there a VPC peering option?
[04:13] Carlos Rivera: Hosted has private-link style connectivity in some regions; Dedicated and Private give you full VPC control. We'll share the network topology doc.
[04:21] Priya Nair: For our unit-econ modelling, we need concrete per-token and per-request latency numbers. Can you run a hosted benchmark with our sample dataset?
[04:30] Carlos Rivera: Yes — request Priya to share 200–500 representative prompts (anonymized) and an expected QPS profile. We'll run a 2k-request batch and return p50/p95 p99 latency and per-token cost. Typically we timebox any benchmark to keep within pilot budget.
[04:45] Priya Nair: I'll share that by Monday.
[04:48] Maya Chen: Great. Quick aside — Elena, for finance — we can model committed discounts. For example, reserved capacity can drive per-token down 20–40% depending on commit. That often tips enterprise deals.
[05:01] Elena Park: Good to know. Also curious about burst handling — if we commit to a base capacity and get an unexpected spike, will you autoscale?
[05:09] Carlos Rivera: Yes autoscaling with burst pools is possible; there's a configurable burst allowance. You can also configure fallback to lower-cost models for non-critical flows.
[05:19] James Holloway: Any notable vendor comparisons? We evaluated OpenAI but their enterprise rate card and batching controls were less flexible; Vertex ties you to a cloud provider. Who else did you see?
[05:29] Maya Chen: We often get compared to OpenAI and Vertex; some customers look at self-managed inference partners like Inferex for on-prem. Each has tradeoffs: OpenAI for simplicity, Vertex for deep cloud integration, Inferex for full self-host control.
[05:41] Priya Nair: Back to numbers — can you share a sample unit-econ for 1M monthly requests with avg 100 input tokens, 80 output tokens and 30% cache?
[05:51] Carlos Rivera: We'll include that in the spreadsheet. Off the cuff, if hosted list-rate is X per 1k tokens, with batching and 30% cache you might see 35–45% effective savings versus naive per-token multiply. Dedicated with quantized models can push to 50–60% savings but requires commit.
[06:10] Elena Park: We need to keep the pilot under $80k — is there an approach to run a meaningful pilot inside that?
[06:16] Maya Chen: Yes. We recommended a 4–6 week pilot: run the 2k-run benchmark (est cost negligible), then a 30-day limited production pilot with capped spend and alerts. We'll propose different pilot bands in the pricing doc to map to $50k / $80k / $120k levels.
[06:32] Priya Nair: Payment terms — do you accept NET 60 for pilots?
[06:36] Maya Chen: For pilots we can be flexible; Enterprise usually goes NET 30 but pilot terms are negotiable. We'll flag procurement.
[06:44] James Holloway: About observability — what telemetry do you expose? Token-level cost, traces per request?
[06:51] Carlos Rivera: We have token-level breakdowns, per-route dashboards, and tracing hooks. You can pull logs into your SIEM via our audit exports.
[07:01] Priya Nair: Any gotchas around quantization and extraction accuracy? We use extraction for high-precision fields; small quality drops are unacceptable for some fields.
[07:10] Carlos Rivera: Understood. We usually run targeted evaluation sets against both FP16 and quantized variants, and we report ROC-style metrics. For sensitive fields we often recommend staying on higher-precision variants until evals pass.
[07:24] Elena Park: Does Redwood charge for KV cache misses? How do you meter cache hits vs misses?
[07:30] Carlos Rivera: Billing is per-token generated and accepted; cache hits reduce tokens generated. We also report cache hit rates in the console so you can model it. There isn't a separate 'cache miss' surcharge — it's just reflected in more tokens used.
[07:44] Priya Nair: If we go Private, what's the timeline and typical infra footprint?
[07:49] Maya Chen: Private typically 8–12 weeks for a base deployment with our package, depends on customer infra and approvals. We'll run a sizing exercise once we have expected QPS and model choice.
[07:59] Priya Nair: For the benchmark, can Redwood run both Hosted and a Dedicated-simulated run so we can compare?
[08:06] Carlos Rivera: We can run hosted and a reserved-capacity test to emulate Dedicated—same model variant and quantization level—so you get apples-to-apples.
[08:14] Maya Chen: Quick logistics, I'll email the pricing template and a short checklist for the benchmark. Carlos will own the test harness. Priya will send the sample prompts and QPS shape. Elena will confirm budget.
[08:26] James Holloway: Any security docs we can review before procurement?
[08:29] Maya Chen: Yes we'll attach SOC 2, encryption docs, network topology and KMS integration notes.
[08:33] Priya Nair: One extra question — for model updates and rollouts, can we pin versions? We need reproducible outputs for audits.
[08:40] Carlos Rivera: Yes you can pin model versions per route. We also support canary/rollout policies and automatic fallback to previous versions.
[08:49] Elena Park: If we want to move to Dedicated after pilot, is there a migration path with minimal downtime?
[08:54] Maya Chen: We support staged migrations: traffic split, canary, and warm-up of Dedicated pools to avoid cold-starts. We'll document the migration runbook.
[09:03] Priya Nair: Good. Anything else around legal or data retention? We need 7-year audit traceability for some records; is that supported?
[09:11] Maya Chen: Audit logs can be exported to your storage and retained per your policy; we support long-term retention as an add-on.
[09:18] James Holloway: Ok that covers most technical things.
[09:21] Maya Chen: Nice. Let's recap next steps — I'll send pricing + SOC 2 + runbook; Carlos will run benchmark once we get prompts; Priya to share prompts; Elena to confirm budget. Any objections or blockers?
[09:34] Priya Nair: No objections. This feels actionable.
[09:36] Elena Park: Sounds good.
[09:38] Maya Chen: Great. We'll shoot for the pricing doc to you by Tuesday. Thanks everyone.

[End of recording]
